children: The Gautam Buddh Nagar court clarified that it had not directed the registration of an FIR and had instead remitted the matter for reconsideration through a reasoned order.

The Gautam Buddh Nagar Sessions Court has set aside an order that treated an application seeking police investigation into an alleged unlawful takeover of a farmhouse as a private complaint, holding that the magistrate had not adequately addressed the material placed before it.
Additional District and Sessions Judge Ashish Kumar Chaurasia allowed the criminal revision filed by Jyoti Kachroo and Robin Raina against the Chief Judicial Magistrate’s order dated 19 May 2025.

The revisionists had moved an application under Section 173(4) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, seeking the registration of an FIR and police investigation into alleged incidents at a farmhouse situated in Agricultural Greens, Greater Noida, during the intervening night of 28 and 29 September 2024.

They alleged unlawful entry, theft, damage to property and forcible possession of the premises. According to the revision petition, movable assets, vehicles and other valuable articles were removed, while a Harley-Davidson motorcycle belonging to Kachroo was subsequently recovered from the possession of one of the respondents.

The revisionists contended that their possession of the property was supported by video material, media reports and a report dated 6 October 2024 prepared by a local commissioner. They argued that the magistrate had rejected the request for police investigation without examining the allegations and supporting material in their entirety.
Respondents Cite Commercial And Arbitration Disputes

The respondents opposed the revision, questioning its maintainability and alleging concealment of material facts. They submitted that the controversy arose from a commercial transaction and was being given a criminal colour. They also referred to proceedings under Sections 9 and 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
The order records that, following a complaint made by Eraaya Lifespaces Limited, the Economic Offences Wing conducted an inquiry and FIR No. 83 of 2025 was registered on 26 June 2025.

The underlying dispute concerns a proposed transaction involving property owned by Firefield Buildcon Private Limited. According to the revisionists, EbixCash Limited had agreed in November 2022 to sell the premises for ₹27 crore, of which ₹20.15 crore had allegedly been transferred. Kachroo claimed ownership and control of Firefield Buildcon and also served as one of its directors.

The Sessions Court observed that its revisional jurisdiction was limited and could not be exercised as though it were hearing an appeal or reassessing the entire evidence. Intervention was nevertheless permissible where the subordinate court’s order disclosed a legal or procedural irregularity.

Referring to the Allahabad High Court’s decision in Sukhwasi v. State of Uttar Pradesh, the court noted that an application seeking police investigation need not result automatically in the registration of an FIR. A magistrate may treat such an application as a complaint, depending on the circumstances.

However, the Sessions Court found that the magistrate’s order did not specifically discuss all the facts presented by the applicants or explain why the matter should proceed only as a private complaint. This omission, it held, amounted to a legal error warranting reconsideration.

The court consequently set aside the order dated 19 May 2025 and directed the magistrate to rehear the parties and pass a fresh, reasoned order in accordance with law. The parties have been directed to appear before the magistrate on 30 October 2026.
The Sessions Court did not express any opinion on the merits of the allegations and did not direct the police to register an FIR.
